tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.
Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.
While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.
Leo used to swimming before school every morning.
By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Maya has finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday.**

Present perfect "has finished" signals a past action with a link to now, but "last Tuesday" is a finished calendar anchor that closes the time frame. In exam English, an explicit finished time (yesterday, last week, in 2019) almost never pairs with present perfect. Repair to past simple: "Maya finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday."

**Trap:** Learners often keep present perfect because the work is "done," forgetting that a named finished day kills that tense.

Finished-time last Tuesday needs past simple, so this doesn’t hold — "Maya finished her chemistry lab report last Tuesday."
**B) Our hiking club has met every Saturday since April.**

Present perfect "has met" with "since April" correctly shows a Saturday habit that began in the past and still continues. The starting point is named, but the period remains open into the present, so present perfect — not past simple — is the right tense. Frequency ("every Saturday") sits comfortably inside that open span.

The open span from April to now is exactly what present perfect marks, so the wording stands.
**C) While the band was rehearsing, the lights suddenly went out.**

Past continuous "was rehearsing" paints the longer background scene; past simple "went out" marks the sudden blackout that cut across it. That continuous-plus-simple pairing is the standard past storytelling pattern for an interrupt. "While" cues the in-progress action, and "suddenly" cues the short past-simple event.

**Tip:** Longer background action → continuous; shorter interrupt → simple past.

Continuous background plus simple interrupt is the right pairing here, so the sentence is sound.
**D) Leo used to swimming before school every morning.**

Past habit needs "used to" + base verb, so "used to swimming" is broken. Repair to "Leo used to swim before school every morning." Do not confuse this with "be used to + -ing," which means familiarity, not past habit — different structure, different meaning.

**Trap:** The -ing form after "used to" feels natural if you mix it up with "be used to doing."

"Used to" takes a bare infinitive, so the line fails; the sound version is "Leo used to swim before school every morning."
**E) By next Friday, the volunteers will plant fifty saplings.**

The cue "by + future time" signals completion before that deadline, which needs future perfect, not plain "will plant." Repair to "By next Friday, the volunteers will have planted fifty saplings." Plain will only talks about a future intention, not that the planting will already be done by Friday.

**Trap:** "Will plant by Friday" looks acceptable in casual speech but fails the exam completion-before-deadline test.

A deadline with by calls for future perfect, so plain will falls short: "By next Friday, the volunteers will have planted fifty saplings."
tasks.solution_overview:
These five lines warm up classic tense traps: finished time versus present perfect with "since," a continuous background interrupted by a sudden event, the form of "used to," and future perfect with "by."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Match each verb to its time cue before you decide. Calendar anchors such as "last Tuesday" usually kill present perfect; "since" keeps a habit alive into the present; "while" often sets a continuous scene for a short past-simple interrupt; "used to" needs a base verb; and "by + future time" often wants future perfect, not plain will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read the highlighted verb against the time expression in the same sentence. If they clash, mark false and name the repair; if they fit the standard pairing, mark true.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.
Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.
I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.
We visited the science museum in March.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The guests already left when the dessert trolley arrived.**

The departure happened before the trolley arrived, so plain past "already left" under-marks the sequence. When two past events stack, mark the earlier one with had + past participle. Repair to past perfect: "The guests had already left when the dessert trolley arrived."

**Trap:** "Already" with past simple looks fine until you notice a second past event that came later.

When departure precedes arrival, past perfect carries the earlier move, so this doesn’t hold — "The guests had already left when the dessert trolley arrived."
**B) They had already left when the dessert trolley arrived.**

Past perfect "had already left" correctly shows that leaving preceded the trolley’s arrival. "Already" sits naturally with past perfect in sequenced past narratives and makes the earlier completion clear. This is the repaired version of the A-line trap.

Past perfect correctly places the earlier leaving before the trolley, so this line holds.
**C) Nina is knowing every lyric in the musical.**

Stative "know" resists continuous form, so "is knowing" is wrong in careful exam English. Mental-state verbs (know, believe, own) rarely take -ing when they report a state rather than a temporary action. Repair to "Nina knows every lyric in the musical."

Stative know stays simple in exam English, so the continuous falls: "Nina knows every lyric in the musical."
**D) I am used to cycling through the park in the rain.**

"Am used to cycling" correctly means accustomed to that rainy-park routine. After "be used to," a gerund is the expected pattern for a recurring activity you find familiar. This is not the same structure as "used to + base verb" for past habit.

**Tip:** "Am/is/are used to + -ing" is familiarity — not past habit.

Familiarity with be used to + -ing fits the rainy-park routine, so the wording stands.
**E) We visited the science museum in March.**

Past simple "visited" with "in March" correctly places a finished outing in a closed time frame. Once the month is named as finished, past simple is the safe default — there is no open link to now that would call for present perfect.

A finished March outing sits cleanly in past simple, so the sentence is sound.
tasks.solution_overview:
This set contrasts past simple with past perfect in a sequenced narrative, tests a stative continuous trap, and separates "be used to" familiarity from ordinary past simple with a closed time frame.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When two past events stack, the earlier one often needs past perfect. Stative verbs such as "know" resist continuous forms. "Be used to + -ing" means accustomed to, which is different from "used to + V1" for past habit. A finished outing with "in March" is safe past simple territory.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask which action happened first, whether the verb is stative, and whether the time frame is still open. Match the verb form to that timeline before you tick true or false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.
By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.
She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.
This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.
We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The coach has changed the starting line-up yesterday evening.**

"Yesterday evening" is finished time, so present perfect "has changed" clashes with the time adverb. Present perfect hates explicit finished-time adverbs in exam answers. Repair to past simple: "The coach changed the starting line-up yesterday evening."

**Trap:** The change still "matters" now, but a finished-time adverb still blocks present perfect.

Yesterday evening closes the frame, so present perfect doesn’t hold — "The coach changed the starting line-up yesterday evening."
**B) By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will pack our bags.**

Completion before a future ferry arrival needs future perfect in the main clause. Plain "will pack" only talks about a future intention, not completion before that docking. Repair to "By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will have packed our bags."

**Trap:** Keeping present "docks" in the time clause fools some writers into keeping plain will in the main clause too.

Completion before the ferry docks wants will have, not plain will: "By the time the ferry docks tomorrow, we will have packed our bags."
**C) She has been a library volunteer here in 2016.**

"In 2016" closes the period, so present perfect "has been" is wrong for that finished role. A named past year usually blocks present perfect because the time frame no longer touches now. Repair to past simple: "She was a library volunteer here in 2016."

A named year like 2016 blocks present perfect, so the line fails — "She was a library volunteer here in 2016."
**D) This scarf is belonging to my grandmother.**

"Belong" is stative, so "is belonging" is wrong. Possession and membership verbs stay in simple forms in formal exam prose. Repair to "This scarf belongs to my grandmother."

Belong is stative, so continuous ownership doesn’t work; the fix is "This scarf belongs to my grandmother."
**E) We used to camp by the lake before the path flooded.**

"Used to camp" correctly reports a discontinued past habit by the lake. The later flood explains why the habit no longer holds, which is exactly what "used to" signals. The base verb after "used to" is the right form for past habit.

Used to + base verb correctly marks the discontinued lake camping habit, so this line holds.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only one sentence survives this card. Hunt finished-time clashes with present perfect, demand future perfect after "by the time," reject a closed year with present perfect, and refuse stative continuous — the lone survivor is clean past habit with "used to."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Yesterday evening" and "in 2016" are finished time and block present perfect. "By the time + future" usually wants will have + past participle. "Belong" is stative and stays simple. "Used to + base verb" correctly reports a discontinued past habit.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline every time cue first. If present perfect or continuous fights that cue, mark false; only keep the line that pairs form and meaning cleanly.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.
While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.
By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.
Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.
Omar is owning three vintage cameras.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The gallery has displayed local artists since the renovation.**

Present perfect "has displayed" with "since the renovation" correctly links an ongoing practice to its start point. The renovation is a starting boundary that still shapes what the gallery does now, so the open span belongs in present perfect.

Since the renovation keeps the gallery practice open into now, present perfect fits and the wording stands.
**B) While the neighbours were gardening, a fox slipped through the fence.**

Past continuous "were gardening" sets the neighbours’ background activity; past simple "slipped" marks the fox’s short interrupt through the fence. That is the standard past pairing for an action in progress when something else struck.

Gardening in progress interrupted by a fox’s slip is classic continuous-plus-simple storytelling, so the sentence is sound.
**C) By year-end, the choir will have learned twelve new pieces.**

Future perfect "will have learned" places completion of the twelve pieces before year-end. The deadline "by" tells you the learning will already be done at that point, which is exactly future perfect’s job.

By year-end names completion ahead of the deadline, and will have learned matches that, so the line holds.
**D) Children used to play outdoors until dusk in this street.**

"Used to play" correctly describes a past outdoor habit that has changed on this street. Frequency through dusk fits the "used to + V1" pattern for discontinued habits. Nothing in the form clashes with the meaning.

Used to play cleanly reports the outdoor dusk habit that has changed, so the wording stands.
**E) Omar is owning three vintage cameras.**

Stative "own" should be simple "owns," not continuous. Ownership verbs almost never take continuous in exam English because they report a state, not a temporary activity. Repair to "Omar owns three vintage cameras."

Own reports a state, not a temporary act, so continuous fails — "Omar owns three vintage cameras."
tasks.solution_overview:
Four sentences are clean; only the stative continuous fails. Confirm "since" with present perfect, background continuous plus interrupt, future perfect with "by," and past habit before you hunt the ownership trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Since" keeps present perfect alive for an ongoing gallery practice. "While" sets a continuous background for a short past-simple interrupt. "By year-end" invites future perfect. "Used to play" is a textbook past habit. "Own" is stative and should not take continuous.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the four standard pairings first; then ask whether the remaining verb is stative. If it is, reject -ing.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week’s briefing.
Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.
The club has published three newsletters this semester.
By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.
When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The weather presenter explained the storm path at last week’s briefing.**

Past simple "explained" correctly anchors a finished talk to "last week’s briefing." The briefing is a closed past event, so past simple is the natural choice. There is no open present link that would invite present perfect.

Last week’s briefing is a closed past event, so past simple explained is the natural fit and the line holds.
**B) Runners are used to training before sunrise in winter.**

"Are used to training" correctly means runners are accustomed to that early-winter routine. The gerund after "be used to" is exactly the familiarity pattern you want here. Do not confuse it with "used to + base verb" for past habit.

**Tip:** "Be used to + -ing" = familiarity, not past habit.

Be used to + training correctly marks winter sunrise familiarity, so the wording stands.
**C) The club has published three newsletters this semester.**

Present perfect "has published" fits an unfinished period ("this semester") with present relevance. The semester is still open, so the three newsletters stay in present perfect rather than past simple.

An unfinished semester keeps the three newsletters in present perfect, so the sentence is sound.
**D) By Friday noon, the caterers will have prepared the picnic baskets.**

Future perfect "will have prepared" correctly places preparation before Friday noon. The clock deadline with "by" is a classic future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that moment.

Friday noon as a completion deadline is textbook future perfect, so will have prepared holds.
**E) When the teacher entered, the class had already finished the quiz.**

Past perfect "had already finished" shows the quiz ended before the teacher walked in. The earlier past action needs had + past participle so the sequence is clear against the when-clause arrival.

The quiz finished earlier than the teacher’s entrance, and past perfect marks that order, so the line is sound.
tasks.solution_overview:
All five lines are sound. Use this card as a model set for closed past time, "be used to," unfinished-period present perfect, future perfect with "by," and past-perfect sequencing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Last week" locks past simple. "Are used to training" means familiarity with a routine. "This semester" keeps present perfect alive. "By Friday noon" wants future perfect. When one past action finishes before another, past perfect marks the earlier one.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each line as a clean template. Confirm the time cue and the verb form agree; do not invent a problem where the pairing is already standard.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I have seen that documentary twice already this month.
They are believing the rumours about the new café.
By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.
Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.
We are knowing each other since primary school.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I have seen that documentary twice already this month.**

Present perfect "have seen" with "already" and an unfinished month fits repeated experience that still matters now. The viewings count toward the current month, so present perfect is right — past simple would close the period too early.

Twice already this month is unfinished time with present relevance, so have seen stands.
**B) They are believing the rumours about the new café.**

"Believe" is stative here, so "are believing" is wrong. Opinion verbs (believe, think = opinion) stay simple in careful exam English when they report a held view. Repair to "They believe the rumours about the new café."

Opinion believe stays simple, so continuous doesn’t hold — "They believe the rumours about the new café."
**C) By dawn, the rescue team will have reached the ridge.**

Future perfect "will have reached" places the team’s arrival before dawn. The cue "by + future point" demands completion ahead of that moment, not merely a plan to reach it at dawn.

Arrival before dawn is prior completion, and will have reached is exactly that pattern, so the wording stands.
**D) Sam used to hate spicy food, but now he loves it.**

"Used to hate" correctly marks a past taste that no longer holds, and the contrast with "now he loves it" makes the change explicit. That is textbook discontinued habit or state with a present contrast.

Used to hate vs now loves makes the discontinued taste explicit, so the sentence is sound.
**E) We are knowing each other since primary school.**

"Know" is stative, and a continuing relationship with "since" needs present perfect, not continuous. Duration with "since" takes present perfect simple for stative verbs. Repair to "We have known each other since primary school."

**Trap:** Continuous looks tempting for a long relationship, but stative "know" + "since" wants have known.

Stative know with since needs have known, not continuous: "We have known each other since primary school."
tasks.solution_overview:
Three survivors and two stative continuous fails. Trust present perfect for unfinished time, future perfect for "by," and "used to" for abandoned habits — then reject -ing on believe and know.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Already" and "this month" support present perfect for repeated experience. Opinion "believe" and stative "know" stay simple (or present perfect for continuing "know"). "By dawn" wants future perfect. "Used to hate" marks a past taste that no longer holds.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First lock the clean tense pairings, then scan for illegally continuous stative verbs — those are the false lines here.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.
The trail was still wet when we have arrived.
I am used to the noise from the tram line.
He used to be afraid of public speaking.
By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Priya has lived in Lisbon for six years.**

Present perfect "has lived" with "for six years" correctly shows a Lisbon situation that continues now. The duration is measured up to the present, which is present-perfect territory rather than a finished past stretch.

Six years of living still true now is classic for + present perfect, so the wording stands.
**B) The trail was still wet when we have arrived.**

A completed arrival inside a past narrative needs past simple, not present perfect. Mixing a past continuous/simple story with present perfect for the same closed past breaks the timeline. Repair to "The trail was still wet when we arrived."

**Trap:** "Have arrived" can feel "recent," but a past narrative locks the arrival in past simple.

A closed past arrival inside a past story takes simple arrived, so this fails — "The trail was still wet when we arrived."
**C) I am used to the noise from the tram line.**

"Am used to the noise" correctly means accustomed to the tram line. After "be used to," a noun works just as well as a gerund — both patterns mark familiarity, not past habit.

**Tip:** After "be used to," use a noun or an -ing form — both are fine.

Be used to + noun correctly marks tram-noise familiarity, so the line holds.
**D) He used to be afraid of public speaking.**

"Used to be afraid" correctly describes a past state of fear that has changed. "Used to + be + adjective" is a clean pattern for former feelings or identities, parallel to "used to + V1" for former habits.

Used to be afraid frames a former state that has changed, so the sentence is sound.
**E) By the time the concert starts, we will have found our seats.**

Future perfect "will have found" places finding seats before the concert begins. Even though the time clause uses present "starts" for future reference, the main clause still needs will have for prior completion.

Finding seats before the concert starts is prior completion, and will have found matches it, so this holds.
tasks.solution_overview:
Watch the one timeline clash: a finished past arrival cannot wear present perfect. Everything else — "for," "be used to," "used to be," and future perfect — is clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Present perfect + "for" shows a situation that continues now. A closed past narrative needs past simple for the arrival, not present perfect. "Be used to" + noun means accustomed to. "Used to be" describes a past state that changed. "By the time + present" for future reference still wants will have in the main clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate open duration and future-before-future from closed past storytelling. Only the mixed past narrative fails.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.
She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.
Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.
We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.
My cousins used to visit us every summer.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The bakery closed early last Sunday because of the heatwave.**

Past simple "closed" with "last Sunday" correctly closes a finished bakery event. The day/date anchor makes past simple the only natural choice — there is no open present span.

Last Sunday anchors a finished bakery event in past simple, so the wording stands.
**B) She has just baked a loaf of sourdough.**

Present perfect "has just baked" marks a recent action with present relevance — the loaf is newly done. "Just" is a classic present-perfect companion in exam English for recent completion that still matters now.

Just with present perfect marks recent baking still relevant now, so the sentence is sound.
**C) Tom is preferring tea to coffee these days.**

"Prefer" is stative, so "is preferring" is wrong. Likes and preferences stay simple unless you force a rare temporary "acting" sense, which exams almost never want. Repair to "Tom prefers tea to coffee these days."

Stative prefer stays simple, so is preferring doesn’t hold — "Tom prefers tea to coffee these days."
**D) We will have walked ten kilometres by lunchtime.**

Future perfect "will have walked" correctly projects ten kilometres covered before lunchtime. Quantity completed by a future point is will have territory rather than plain will walk.

Ten kilometres covered before lunchtime is future-perfect territory, so will have walked holds.
**E) My cousins used to visit us every summer.**

"Used to visit" correctly reports a repeated past summer habit. Frequency phrases such as "every summer" sit naturally with "used to" when the visits no longer happen (or are framed as former habit).

Every-summer visits framed as former habit sit cleanly with used to visit, so the line is sound.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four good lines and one stative continuous. Separate closed past ("last Sunday") from recent present perfect ("just"), keep future perfect and past habit, then reject "is preferring."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Day anchors such as "last Sunday" lock past simple. "Just" marks a recent action with present relevance in present perfect. "Prefer" is stative and stays simple. Distance covered "by lunchtime" wants future perfect. Frequency phrases sit naturally with "used to."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Confirm each time cue against its usual tense, then scan preferences and likes for illegal continuous forms.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Did you ever climb a volcano?
Have you ever climbed a volcano?
While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.
They are used to get up early for rowing practice.
By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Did you ever climb a volcano?**

Life experience up to now needs present perfect in careful exam English. Past simple "Did you ever" is non-standard for open lifetime experience when no finished period is named. Repair to "Have you ever climbed a volcano?"

**Trap:** "Did you ever…?" is common in casual speech, so it looks almost right on the page.

Open lifetime experience wants Have you ever, not Did you ever, in exam English — "Have you ever climbed a volcano?"
**B) Have you ever climbed a volcano?**

Present perfect "Have you ever climbed" correctly asks about experience at any time up to now. "Ever" with present perfect is the standard life-experience pattern, contrasting with the broken A-line.

**Tip:** "Ever / never" + present perfect = life experience.

Ever with present perfect is the standard life-experience question, so the wording stands.
**C) While I was reading on the balcony, it started to snow.**

Past continuous "was reading" sets the balcony background; past simple "started" marks the snow interrupt. Reading was in progress; snow was the sudden change — the standard while-pairing.

Reading in progress interrupted by snow is continuous background plus simple interrupt, so the sentence is sound.
**D) They are used to get up early for rowing practice.**

Familiarity needs "be used to" + -ing (or a noun), never a bare infinitive. Repair to "They are used to getting up early for rowing practice." The bare infinitive after "be used to" is a classic mix-up with "used to get up" (past habit).

**Trap:** "Are used to get" blends familiarity "be used to" with habit "used to + V1."

Be used to needs -ing, not a bare infinitive, so the form fails: "They are used to getting up early for rowing practice."
**E) By next winter, she will have completed her first marathon.**

Future perfect "will have completed" places marathon completion before next winter. Seasonal "by next …" deadlines routinely take will have + past participle for prior completion.

Marathon completion before next winter is future perfect’s job, so will have completed holds.
tasks.solution_overview:
Compare the two experience questions side by side, keep the continuous–simple pair, fix "be used to" + -ing, and lock future perfect with "by next winter."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Lifetime experience up to now needs present perfect with "ever," not past simple "Did you ever" in careful exam English. Background continuous plus simple interrupt stays textbook. After "be used to," you need a gerund, never a bare infinitive. "By next winter" wants future perfect.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat A and B as a minimal pair, then check gerund form after "be used to" and the future-perfect deadline.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The app update has crashed twice since midnight.
I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.
We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.
By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.
Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The app update has crashed twice since midnight.**

Present perfect "has crashed" with "since midnight" fits repeated glitches that still matter now. Tech problems counted from a start point into the present stay in present perfect rather than a closed past count.

Crashes counted from midnight into now stay in present perfect, so the wording stands.
**B) I was understanding the lecture until the fire alarm rang.**

"Understand" is stative, so "was understanding" is wrong in exam English. Use past simple for the sense before the interrupt: "I understood the lecture until the fire alarm rang." Stative verbs rarely take past continuous in exam answers.

**Trap:** Continuous seems to match "until," but stative "understand" still wants simple form.

Understand is stative, so was understanding fails — "I understood the lecture until the fire alarm rang."
**C) We used to take the coastal path before the landslide.**

"Used to take" correctly marks a coastal-path habit that ended after the landslide. A later change that blocks the old routine is exactly what "used to" signals, with the base verb in place.

A coastal-path habit ended by the landslide is textbook used to + base verb, so the sentence is sound.
**D) By eight o’clock, the photographer will have set up the lights.**

Future perfect "will have set up" places the lighting ready before eight o’clock. A clock deadline with "by" is a classic future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that time.

Lights ready before eight o’clock is prior completion by a clock point, so will have set up holds.
**E) Hana has known her climbing partner for a decade.**

Present perfect "has known" with "for a decade" correctly shows a continuing relationship. For stative "know," duration up to now takes have/has known — never "am knowing" or other continuous forms.

**Tip:** "Have known … for" beats any continuous "knowing."

A decade of knowing up to now takes has known, not continuous knowing, so the line is sound.
tasks.solution_overview:
Four keepers and one stative continuous. Trust "since," "used to," future perfect, and "have known" — reject "was understanding."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Present perfect with "since midnight" fits repeated crashes still relevant now. "Understand" is stative and rarely takes past continuous in exams. "Used to take" marks a discontinued route. Clock "by" wants future perfect. Stative "know" with "for" takes present perfect simple.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Approve the four standard tense pairings, then ask whether continuous is trying to attach to a stative verb — that is the false line.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.
When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.
She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.
I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.
They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.
tactical_explanations:
**A) When we reached the summit, the sun has already risen.**

Both events are in the past, so the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect. Closed past narrative wants had + V3 for the action that finished first. Repair to "When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen."

**Trap:** "Already" tempts present perfect, but a finished past story still needs past perfect for the earlier event.

In a finished past summit story the earlier sunrise needs had, not has: "When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen."
**B) When we reached the summit, the sun had already risen.**

Past perfect "had already risen" correctly places sunrise before the summit arrival. "Already" with past perfect marks the prior completed state clearly against the when-clause past simple.

Past perfect correctly places sunrise before the summit arrival, so this line holds.
**C) She is seeming tired after the long rehearsal.**

"Seem" is stative, so "is seeming" is wrong. Appearance verbs (seem, appear = look like) stay simple in exam prose when they report how someone looks or comes across. Repair to "She seems tired after the long rehearsal."

Seem is stative, so is seeming doesn’t work — "She seems tired after the long rehearsal."
**D) I am getting used to the new keyboard layout.**

"Getting used to" correctly means becoming accustomed to the new keyboard. This is the process of adapting, which differs from "be used to" (already adapted). Continuous "getting" fits that in-progress adaptation.

**Tip:** "Get used to" = adapting; "be used to" = already familiar.

Getting used to marks adapting in progress, which matches the new keyboard, so the wording stands.
**E) They will have reheated the soup by the time you arrive.**

Future perfect "will have reheated" places the reheating before your arrival. "By the time you arrive" is a standard cue for will have + past participle in the main clause.

Soup reheated before your arrival is will have + V3 after by the time, so the sentence is sound.
tasks.solution_overview:
Contrast the two summit lines carefully, reject stative "seeming," and accept "get used to" plus future perfect as clean.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

In a closed past narrative, the earlier sunrise needs past perfect, not present perfect. "Seem" is stative and stays simple. "Get used to" means becoming accustomed — the process of adapting. "By the time you arrive" wants will have in the main clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read A and B as a minimal pair for past perfect versus present perfect, then check stative continuous and the adapting / future-perfect lines.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

tactical_explanations:
**A) How long are you waiting for the night bus?**

**Trap:** Present continuous answers "what now?" but not "for how long up to now?"

How long for an ongoing wait needs have been waiting, not plain present continuous: "How long have you been waiting for the night bus?"
**B) How long have you been waiting for the night bus?**

Present perfect continuous "have you been waiting" correctly asks about waiting that started earlier and continues. Visible temporary activity plus duration is exactly this form’s job — the repaired pair to A.

Waiting that began earlier and continues is present perfect continuous territory, so the wording stands.
**C) The river flooded the towpath three times last winter.**

Past simple "flooded" with "last winter" correctly counts finished floods in a closed season. Numbered past events inside a finished period take past simple, not present perfect.

Three floods inside a finished last winter sit in past simple, so the sentence is sound.
**D) Jonas used to living near the botanical gardens.**

Past habit needs "used to live," not "used to living." Never put -ing after "used to" when you mean habit — that -ing pattern belongs to "be used to." Repair to "Jonas used to live near the botanical gardens."

**Trap:** "Used to living" mixes past-habit "used to" with familiarity "be used to + -ing."

Past habit is used to live, never used to living — "Jonas used to live near the botanical gardens."
**E) By Thursday evening, we will have curated the exhibition labels.**

Future perfect "will have curated" places the labels ready before Thursday evening. An art-deadline "by" is another future-perfect cue for completion ahead of that point.

Labels curated before Thursday evening is deadline completion, so will have curated holds.

Duration questions need present perfect continuous, closed seasons need past simple, and "used to" never takes -ing for habit. Future perfect with "by" stays solid.

Compare the two duration questions as a pair, then check the past-season count, the "used to" form, and the curation deadline.

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

Idiomatic have been meaning to covers the week-long delayed call, so the wording stands.
**B) This jacket is fitting me perfectly today.**

Size fit is stative, so is fitting fails — "This jacket fits me perfectly today."
**C) We had finished dinner before the guests rang the doorbell.**

Past perfect "had finished" correctly shows dinner ended before the doorbell. The word "before" helps you spot which past action is earlier and keeps the sequence clear with past simple for the later ring.

Dinner ending before the doorbell is the earlier past, and had finished marks it, so the line holds.
**D) She is used to cook for large family gatherings.**

Familiarity needs "is used to cooking," not "is used to cook." After "be used to," use -ing or a noun — never a bare infinitive. Repair by swapping the bare infinitive for a gerund.

**Trap:** Bare infinitive after "be used to" is a near-miss blend with "used to cook."

After be used to, cooking (not cook) carries familiarity: "She is used to cooking for large family gatherings."
**E) By the time the podcast drops, the host will have recorded three more episodes.**

Future perfect "will have recorded" places the three extra episodes before the podcast drops. Release schedules with "by the time" routinely take will have for prior completion in the main clause.

Three more episodes done before the podcast drops is future perfect after by the time, so the sentence is sound.

Accept the idiomatic "have been meaning," keep past perfect and future perfect, and reject stative "fitting" plus the bare infinitive after "be used to."

Keep the idiomatic and sequencing lines; fail only the stative continuous and the broken "be used to" pattern.

tasks.title: Task 14

**E) By noon tomorrow, the drones will have mapped the whole coastline.**

Future perfect "will have mapped" places coastline mapping complete before noon tomorrow. Science deadlines with "by" take will have + past participle for prior completion.

Pair the "since" lines carefully, keep "used to" and future perfect, and notice when a sense verb becomes dynamic ("am tasting") so continuous is fine.

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.

tactical_explanations:
**A) He has gone to the allotment — he should be back by dusk.**

"Has gone" correctly means he went to the allotment and is still away, with return expected by dusk. The present result is absence, which is what "has gone" encodes — unlike "has been," which would imply a completed visit and return.

**Tip:** Has gone = left and not back yet.

Has gone correctly leaves him still at the allotment with return by dusk, so the line holds.
**B) He has been to the allotment three times this week.**

"Has been to" correctly means visited and returned — three completed visits this week. That experience/count reading is different from "has gone," which would leave him still there. The unfinished week keeps present perfect natural.

**Tip:** Has been to = visited; has gone to = still there.

Has been to counts completed visits and returns this week, so the wording stands.
**C) We are loving this new pottery class.**

In careful exam English, "love" stays stative. Marketing "I’m loving it" is too informal for the default exam standard. Repair to "We love this new pottery class."

**Trap:** Advertising continuous "loving" is familiar in speech but fails careful exam style.

Careful exam English keeps love simple, so are loving fails — "We love this new pottery class."
**D) They will have been travelling for fourteen hours by the time they land.**

Future perfect continuous "will have been travelling" correctly stresses fourteen hours of travel completed before landing. Duration up to a future point is will have been + -ing territory rather than plain future continuous.

**Tip:** "By the time" + duration → will have been + -ing.

Fourteen hours of travel up to landing is will have been travelling, so the sentence is sound.
**E) I used to be used to the cold winters, but I am not any more.**

The sentence deliberately contrasts "used to be" (a past state of cold-hardiness) with "be used to" (familiarity) and uses both forms correctly. The closing "I am not any more" shows the familiarity has ended, which justifies stacking the two patterns.

**Tip:** Used to be ≠ be used to; combining them is fine when meaning needs both.

Stacking used to be with be used to correctly contrasts past hardiness and lost familiarity, so this holds.
tasks.solution_overview:
Master "gone" versus "been," reject informal continuous "loving," accept future perfect continuous for duration, and parse the double "used to" contrast carefully.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Has gone" means left and still away; "has been to" means visited and returned. In careful exam English, "love" stays stative. Duration before landing wants will have been + -ing. You can correctly combine "used to be" (past state) with "be used to" (familiarity) when the meaning requires both.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Separate the allotment pair first, reject marketing-style "are loving," then confirm duration and the nested used-to contrast.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

I wish + past perfect correctly frames yesterday’s packing regret, so the wording stands.
**C) She has been working on the mural all morning and still isn’t finished.**

Present perfect continuous "has been working" correctly stresses mural work that has run all morning and is still unfinished. Duration plus "still isn’t finished" is classic have been + -ing for activity stretching into now.

All-morning unfinished mural work stretches into now with has been working, so the sentence is sound.
**D) The soup is smelling of garlic and thyme right now.**

"Is smelling" reports a temporary sensory impression right now, so continuous is natural. The dynamic sense (how the soup smells at this moment) can take -ing; stative "It smells of garlic" would also be fine as an alternative.

Fix the wish-regret pattern, then accept present perfect continuous, a dynamic sensory continuous, and future perfect continuous for long-running volunteering.

Treat A/B as the regret minimal pair, then confirm the three advanced continuous patterns on C–E.

**B) It’s high time we updated the club website.**

Past perfect "had passed" marks the earlier storm; past simple "began" covers the later singing. After + past perfect, then simple past for the next event, is a clean sequence of two past stages.

Fail only the broken high-time line; keep B–E as clean advanced patterns.

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

tactical_explanations:
**A) No sooner the train had left than the platform announcement began.**

**Trap:** Keeping "the train had" after "no sooner" looks almost grammatical until you check inversion.

**B) No sooner had the train left than the platform announcement began.**

**Tip:** No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than…

Inverted no sooner had … than … correctly chains train and announcement, so the wording stands.
**C) I have yet to try the new climbing wall downtown.**

"Have yet to try" is a present-perfect pattern meaning you still have not done it. The climbing wall remains outstanding experience, which is exactly what the construction encodes.

**Tip:** Have yet to + base verb = still outstanding.

Have yet to try correctly leaves the climbing wall still undone, so the sentence is sound.
**D) We are having a brilliant time at the street festival.**

"Are having" for enjoyment is dynamic, so continuous is fine — you are experiencing the festival, not "owning" a time. Contrast this with stative possession "have," which stays simple.

**Tip:** Having a good time / having lunch = action; owning = stative.

Experiential having a brilliant time is dynamic, so continuous is fine and the line holds.
**E) By the time you read this postcard, we will already arrive in Lisbon.**

**Trap:** "Already" next to will feels complete, but "by the time" still wants will have.

By the time needs future perfect for already-done arrival: "By the time you read this postcard, we will already have arrived in Lisbon."

Force inversion after "no sooner," keep "have yet to" and dynamic "having," and repair the broken future perfect after "by the time."

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"No sooner" needs auxiliary inversion: No sooner had + subject + V3 + than. "Have yet to" means still have not done something. Experiential "having a brilliant time" is dynamic, so continuous is fine. "By the time" with a future reading needs will have, not plain will arrive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Compare A/B as the inversion minimal pair, keep C/D, and fix E's missing future perfect.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20

Inverted hardly had … when … correctly places sitting just before the buzz, so the wording stands.
**C) She has been wanting a pottery wheel for months.**
